chunks: Chip fabrication yield considerations. The question: Describe any yield considerations when fabricating chips.
Yield is the fraction of chips that work. On a wafer, random flaws such as dust specks and scratches land here and there, and a die is ruined if a serious flaw lands on it.
A bigger die has more area to be hit, so yield falls quickly as dies get larger. That is why big chips cost so much more than small ones.
Flick a few drops of paint at random across a sheet of postage stamps. Every stamp that gets a spot is spoiled. If the stamps are tiny, most escape.
If each stamp is the size of a poster, nearly all get hit. A wafer is the sheet, the dies are the stamps, and the paint spots are the flaws.
Real flaws sometimes clump together, which helps big dies a little.
Each box removes some units.

The first box loses whole wafers, the second loses dies to defects, the third loses dies that work but miss specs (which binning can partly recover), and the last two lose parts to packaging and test.
The product of the stage yields is the number the business cares about.
Yield: the fraction of units that work. Defect: a flaw (dust, scratch, process slip) that ruins a die.
Defect density: how many serious defects land per square centimeter of wafer. Die: one chip's worth of silicon cut from a wafer.
Binning: sorting working chips by speed and selling them as different grades. Redundancy: spare parts built into a chip, so one defect does not ruin it.
Say the defect density is 0. 1 per cm². A 1 cm² die expects 0. 1 defects. A 6 cm² die expects 0. 6.
The chance of getting no defect is e to the -x , where x is the expected number and e is a fixed number, about 2. 718 (a calculator has a button for it).
So the 1 cm² die yields about 90%, and the 6 cm² die about 55%. And yield is only part of the damage for the big die: far fewer of them fit on each wafer, too.
That is the whole idea.

Designers respond with smaller dies or chiplets, redundancy, binning, design-for-yield rules, while the foundry drives defect density down as the process matures."
